topics.title: Graphs
topics.subject: mathematics
outcomes: plot and draw lines through given points. (u, s)
choose and uses appropriate scales. (u, s)
draw, read and interpret the graph (e.g. Distance-Time and Speed-Time Graphs to estimate distance, speed and time). (u, s, v/a)

body.text: A night bus leaves Soroti at 20:30 and reaches Kampala at 04:00, stopping at towns on the way. A table of times tells the story in numbers. A graph tells it as a picture, so we can see at a glance where the bus moved fast and where it waited.

A relation such as y = 2x + 1 links each value of x to a value of y. To draw its graph, first make a table of values. Choose some values of x. Work out y for each one. Each pair of values gives a point (x, y).

body.title: Tabulate and plot y = 2x + 1
steps: Plot each point with a small cross. Join them with one straight line drawn with a ruler. Label the line y = 2x + 1.

body.text: If one point does not lie on the line with the others, check its value in the table. A relation of the form y = mx + c always gives a straight line.
The scale tells us how many units each centimetre or each square on the paper stands for. A good scale makes the graph large and easy to read.

items: Use a scale that makes the graph fill most of the paper.
Choose easy steps such as 1, 2, 5, 10 or 20 units for each centimetre. Avoid steps of 3 or 7, which are hard to read.
The two axes may have different scales.
Label each axis with the quantity and its unit, and give the graph a title.

body.title: Draw and use a temperature conversion graph
steps: The rule for changing degrees Celsius (°C) to degrees Fahrenheit (°F) is F = 9C ÷ 5 + 32.
The paper is 16 cm wide and 24 cm tall. Across, let 1 cm stand for 10 °C, so 0 to 100 °C takes 10 cm. Up, let 1 cm stand for 10 °F, so 0 to 212 °F takes about 22 cm.
Plot the four points and join them with a straight line.
To change 30 °C, go up from 30 on the Celsius axis to the line, then across to the Fahrenheit axis. It reads 86 °F.

body.text: A distance–time graph shows a journey. Time goes along the horizontal axis. Distance from the start goes up the vertical axis. A straight sloping line means steady speed. A steeper line means a higher speed. A horizontal line means the traveller has stopped, because time passes but the distance does not change.

body.speech: speed equals distance divided by time

body.title: The Soroti to Mbale part of the bus journey
steps: The bus leaves Soroti at 20:30. It reaches Kumi, 50 km away, at 22:00. It waits and leaves at 22:15. It reaches Mbale, 56 km beyond Kumi, at 23:30.
Points to plot (time, distance from Soroti): (20:30, 0 km), (22:00, 50 km), (22:15, 50 km), (23:30, 106 km).
Soroti to Kumi: 50 km in 1 hour 30 minutes = 1.5 hours. Speed = 50 ÷ 1.5 ≈ 33.3 km/h.
At Kumi the line is flat for 15 minutes while the bus waits.
Kumi to Mbale: 56 km in 1 hour 15 minutes = 1.25 hours. Speed = 56 ÷ 1.25 = 44.8 km/h.
The Kumi to Mbale line is steeper, so the bus moved faster on that part.

body.title: Read a walk from a graph
steps: Atim's graph rises from 0 km at 09:00 to 2 km at 09:30. It stays flat at 2 km until 10:30. It falls back to 0 km at 11:10.
She walked 2 km to her friend's house in 30 minutes. Speed = 2 ÷ 0.5 = 4 km/h.
She stayed there for 1 hour.
She walked home in 40 minutes, which is 40 ÷ 60 = 2/3 of an hour. Speed = 2 ÷ 2/3 = 3 km/h.
The line going home is less steep, so she walked back more slowly.

body.text: A speed–time graph has time along the horizontal axis and speed up the vertical axis. A horizontal line now means steady speed, not stopping. A rising line means speeding up. The area under a speed–time graph gives the distance travelled.

body.title: Find a distance from a speed–time graph
steps: A taxi leaves a stage. Its speed rises steadily from 0 to 20 m/s in 10 seconds. It then moves at 20 m/s for 30 seconds.
The first part of the graph is a triangle with base 10 s and height 20 m/s. Area = ½ × 10 × 20 = 100 m.
The second part is a rectangle 30 s long and 20 m/s high. Area = 30 × 20 = 600 m.
Total distance = 100 + 600 = 700 m.

body.title: Walk a graph
body.text: On the school compound, mark a straight 50 m path with a stick every 10 m. One learner walks slowly for 20 m, stands still for 10 seconds, then walks quickly to the end. Others use a watch or phone to record the time at each stick. Make a table, choose scales and draw the distance–time graph. Point to where the walker stopped and where the walker was fastest.
What would a vertical line on a distance–time graph mean? Could a real journey ever make one? Why can the line on a distance–time graph never slope back to the left?

Make a table of values, choose clear scales, plot the points and join them carefully. On a distance–time graph, steeper means faster, a flat line means stopped, and speed = distance ÷ time. On a speed–time graph, a flat line means steady speed and the area underneath gives the distance travelled.
